cells.tense: You are keeping something steady right now, and you are doing it on purpose, not by accident.
cells.ask: Give one thing you've kept steady to the person it would matter to, and let it change hands.
cells.core:
You're keeping something steady, and it's deliberate. Not gripping it and not letting it slide — you hold it the way you hold something that still carries weight, and it holds back. What change produced is intact, and you can see its shape clearly enough to know what it needs from you next.

Going well, this looks like a light hand: something still useful, still yours, passed along to someone who can use it, and something coming back without armor on. That exchange is what keeps a kept thing alive. Check what returns — whether it's real, whether it's fair. That look is part of it too, and it costs you the comfort of not asking.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something steady, and the steadying is on purpose.

cells.tense: You are standing in front of a future that hasn't happened, guarding it like it's yours to defend.
cells.ask: Let one thing you're protecting stay unguarded today. Leave it where it is and do nothing to it.
cells.core:
You're guarding something that hasn't happened yet. The shape of a future loss got vivid, and you've been standing at the door holding it off — checking, bracing, taking the weight early. What's here is fine, and you can see how it stays fine without your arm against the door.

Notice what's actually in front of you before deciding it needs defending. One thing you're treating as fragile can go unattended today. You'll find out whether it needed you at all, and you can keep the recognition of what's real without swallowing what isn't yours to carry. That's the way back to holding only what's here, and it means letting some guard duty go unfilled.
cells.sheetLine: You're guarding a future that hasn't arrived, and it costs you the present.

cells.tense: You were part of something that settled, and part of you stayed at a door already closed.
cells.ask: Pick one thing still here after the change and do the small next thing with it today.
cells.core:
Something ended and you didn't finish walking away from it. Not that you don't care — that you care and stopped moving. You're still turned toward what changed, waiting to be told it's okay to let it be finished, while the thing you kept sits there fine without instructions.

Pick something that survived and do the next small thing with it, without waiting to feel ready first. Movement will steady you — direction comes from doing, not from certainty. Feed what moves instead of forcing feeling into where it went quiet, and the rest catches up on its own timing. Waiting for permission is the part that keeps you turned around.
cells.sheetLine: You're standing in a doorway that's already behind you.

cells.tense: You are already the one keeping it steady, and you describe it as staying that way by itself.
cells.ask: About one thing you've kept steady, say out loud that you're the one holding it.
cells.core:
You're the one keeping this in place. When it holds, it holds because you keep it holding — and the way you tell it, it simply works that way. You can see the structure beneath the surface: what rests on what, which part would give if you stopped. That's a clear reading of how things work, and you run it without claiming it.

Say it. One thing you've kept steady, name it as yours out loud once. Not to take credit from anyone else — to stop handing off the making of something you make. The ground under your feet gets more solid for it, and the people around you get something truer to stand on too.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it steady. Say so.
